before.label: Economic history
before.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000).

strands.focus: Economic life studied through social relations, belief, households, and women’s work.
strands.works: Tawney, Religion and the Rise of Capitalism; Power, Medieval People; Clark and Pinchbeck on women’s labour

strands.focus: Simiand and Labrousse investigate different economic movements. Later rereadings distinguish construction of evidence, causal conditions and routine series; uneven crises need not fit one automatic sequence.

strands.title: Capitalist development and contested production relations
strands.focus: Coercion, markets, wage labour and the state are related explanatory problems. Dobb’s reply acknowledges uncertainty about one accumulation hypothesis; Sweezy and Takahashi pose different challenges.
strands.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167; Takahashi (1952); Unwin (1904)

strands.title: Cliometrics and historical measurement
strands.focus: Economic models and quantitative evidence; neither all economic history nor all quantitative history.
strands.works: Fogel, “Economic Growth, Population Theory, and Physiology” (1993); North, “Economic Performance through Time” (1993)

strands.title: Institutions and economic change
strands.focus: Rules, incentives, learning, and historical paths; overlaps with cliometrics without being identical to it.
strands.works: North, Economic Performance through Time

strands.title: Slavery, empire, and unequal development
strands.focus: Different arguments about capitalist development and colonial power; Drescher contests the decline explanation for British slave-trade abolition.
strands.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972); Econocide (1977)

strands.title: Market society and nonmarket economic relations
strands.focus: Polanyi distinguishes a market-regulated economy from reciprocity and redistribution; his broad historical claims are arguments to examine, not settled descriptions of every society.
strands.works: The Great Transformation (1944), chapter IV

strands.title: Different paths of later industrialization
strands.focus: Compare technology borrowing, industrial scale and the roles of banks and states; later industrializers need not repeat England’s sequence.
strands.works: Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection)

strands.title: Household labor, demand and industrious change
strands.focus: Changes in household resource allocation can increase market labor and demand together. Household members’ interests differ, and the proposed pattern is not universal.
strands.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

strands.title: Regional comparison and global divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz compares developed regions within Eurasia and connects divergence with coal and overseas resources, avoiding an undifferentiated Europe-versus-Asia contrast.
strands.works: The Great Divergence (2000)

strands.title: Material life, markets and capitalism
strands.focus: Braudel distinguishes overlapping economic activities and geographically centered world-economies. His disagreement with Weber and selective Wallerstein dialogue are attributed arguments, not a settled universal history.
strands.works: Afterthoughts on Material Civilization and Capitalism (1977)

strands.title: Market norms and popular action
strands.focus: Thompson asks how customary expectations authorize or constrain protest and exchange; Mintz supplies a named anthropological resource. This is a situated inquiry into English crowds, not a universal premarket economy.
strands.works: “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

strands.title: Agrarian change and documentary comparability
strands.focus: Tawney distinguishes regional and temporal patterns, tenant and landlord activity, legal forms and economic pressures. His introduction treats incomplete statistics and incompatible records as problems of inference.
strands.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

strands.title: Women’s work, household forms and economic change
strands.focus: Clark and Pinchbeck distinguish home production from wages, while differing over the timing and consequences of economic change. Their acknowledgments make research guidance and shared materials part of this scholarship.
strands.works: Working Life of Women (1919); Women Workers (1930)

strands.title: Domestic service as an economic question
strands.focus: Salmon connects household employment with industrial specialization and challenges its reduction to a private complaint. Her historical model and proposed remedies are arguments to assess, not a universal account of women’s experience.
strands.works: Domestic Service (1897), chapters I–II; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

strands.title: Brazilian income flows and structural criticism
strands.focus: Furtado’s coffee-crisis argument connects demand and historical change; Novais asks how wage labour and capitalism’s formation explain the transformation. Their exchange keeps macroeconomic analysis open to historical criticism.
strands.works: Furtado (1959/2005), XXXI–XXXII opening; Novais (1961)

strands.title: Managerial coordination and the scale of activity
strands.focus: Chandler’s selected opening links new energy, transport and communication capacities to the conditions for administrative coordination. Earlier growth and specialization could remain compatible with owner-managed firms and market exchange.
strands.works: The Visible Hand (1977), Part I and chapter1 opening

strands.title: Artisans and uneven industrialization in India
strands.focus: Roy examines five crafts rather than treating textile decline as universal. His introduction distinguishes family work, wage labour, markets and organizational change, while acknowledging that adaptation did not yield development comparable to Europe or Japan.
strands.works: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India (1999), introduction

strands.title: Firms, inventions and forms of work
strands.focus: Compare Chandler’s American enterprise scale, Mokyr’s British technological change and Roy’s Indian artisanal reorganization. These explanations concern different units and periods; none supplies a universal sequence from household to large factory.
strands.works: Chandler (1977); Mokyr (1999); Roy (1999), selected primary passages

before.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

strands.title: French serial and conjunctural history
strands.focus: Simiand and Labrousse investigate different economic movements. Later rereadings distinguish construction of evidence, causal conditions and routine series; uneven crises need not fit one automatic sequence.
strands.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933); La crise de l’économie française à la fin de l’Ancien Régime et au début de la Révolution (1944); “Panoramas de la crise” (1956); Grenier/Lepetit (1989); Simonin (1992)

strands.title: Capitalist development and contested production relations
strands.focus: Coercion, markets, wage labour and the state are related explanatory problems. Dobb’s reply acknowledges uncertainty about one accumulation hypothesis; Sweezy and Takahashi pose different challenges.
strands.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167; Takahashi (1952); Unwin (1904)

strands.title: Cliometrics and historical measurement
strands.focus: Economic models and quantitative evidence; neither all economic history nor all quantitative history.
strands.works: Fogel, “Economic Growth, Population Theory, and Physiology” (1993); North, “Economic Performance through Time” (1993)

strands.title: Institutions and economic change
strands.focus: Rules, incentives, learning, and historical paths; overlaps with cliometrics without being identical to it.
strands.works: North, Economic Performance through Time

strands.title: Slavery, empire, and unequal development
strands.focus: Different arguments about capitalist development and colonial power; Drescher contests the decline explanation for British slave-trade abolition.
strands.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972); Econocide (1977)

strands.title: Market society and nonmarket economic relations
strands.focus: Polanyi distinguishes a market-regulated economy from reciprocity and redistribution; his broad historical claims are arguments to examine, not settled descriptions of every society.
strands.works: The Great Transformation (1944), chapter IV

strands.title: Different paths of later industrialization
strands.focus: Compare technology borrowing, industrial scale and the roles of banks and states; later industrializers need not repeat England’s sequence.
strands.works: Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection)

strands.title: Household labor, demand and industrious change
strands.focus: Changes in household resource allocation can increase market labor and demand together. Household members’ interests differ, and the proposed pattern is not universal.
strands.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

strands.title: Regional comparison and global divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz compares developed regions within Eurasia and connects divergence with coal and overseas resources, avoiding an undifferentiated Europe-versus-Asia contrast.
strands.works: The Great Divergence (2000)

strands.title: Material life, markets and capitalism
strands.focus: Braudel distinguishes overlapping economic activities and geographically centered world-economies. His disagreement with Weber and selective Wallerstein dialogue are attributed arguments, not a settled universal history.
strands.works: Afterthoughts on Material Civilization and Capitalism (1977)

strands.title: Market norms and popular action
strands.focus: Thompson asks how customary expectations authorize or constrain protest and exchange; Mintz supplies a named anthropological resource. This is a situated inquiry into English crowds, not a universal premarket economy.
strands.works: “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

strands.title: Agrarian change and documentary comparability
strands.focus: Tawney distinguishes regional and temporal patterns, tenant and landlord activity, legal forms and economic pressures. His introduction treats incomplete statistics and incompatible records as problems of inference.
strands.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

strands.title: Women’s work, household forms and economic change
strands.focus: Clark and Pinchbeck distinguish home production from wages, while differing over the timing and consequences of economic change. Their acknowledgments make research guidance and shared materials part of this scholarship.
strands.works: Working Life of Women (1919); Women Workers (1930)

strands.title: Domestic service as an economic question
strands.focus: Salmon connects household employment with industrial specialization and challenges its reduction to a private complaint. Her historical model and proposed remedies are arguments to assess, not a universal account of women’s experience.
strands.works: Domestic Service (1897), chapters I–II; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

strands.title: Brazilian income flows and structural criticism
strands.focus: Furtado’s coffee-crisis argument connects demand and historical change; Novais asks how wage labour and capitalism’s formation explain the transformation. Their exchange keeps macroeconomic analysis open to historical criticism.
strands.works: Furtado (1959/2005), XXXI–XXXII opening; Novais (1961)

strands.title: Managerial coordination and the scale of activity
strands.focus: Chandler’s selected opening links new energy, transport and communication capacities to the conditions for administrative coordination. Earlier growth and specialization could remain compatible with owner-managed firms and market exchange.
strands.works: The Visible Hand (1977), Part I and chapter1 opening

strands.title: Artisans and uneven industrialization in India
strands.focus: Roy examines five crafts rather than treating textile decline as universal. His introduction distinguishes family work, wage labour, markets and organizational change, while acknowledging that adaptation did not yield development comparable to Europe or Japan.
strands.works: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India (1999), introduction

strands.title: Firms, inventions and forms of work
strands.focus: Compare Chandler’s American enterprise scale, Mokyr’s British technological change and Roy’s Indian artisanal reorganization. These explanations concern different units and periods; none supplies a universal sequence from household to large factory.
strands.works: Chandler (1977); Mokyr (1999); Roy (1999), selected primary passages

strands.title: Railroads and the meaning of social saving
strands.focus: McClelland contests identifying measured transport savings with the railroad’s entire contribution to growth. His notes question the relation between observed freight prices and marginal costs under altered traffic and competition.
strands.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); McClelland (1968), opening and notes

strands.title: Slavery productivity and a contested inference
strands.focus: Fogel and Engerman’s opening specifies a total-factor-productivity index. David and Temin argue that national-price aggregation across differing crop mixes need not rank technical efficiency: climate, prices and risk complicate the inference.
strands.works: Fogel/Engerman (1977), opening; David/Temin (1979),213–214

after.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

before.label: Quantitative history
before.description: Uses serial evidence, linked records, statistics and explicit models to ask different historical questions. Labrousse’s prices, Henry’s reconstructed families, Benson’s voting groups, Thernstrom’s mobility and Curtin’s slave-trade estimates extend beyond cliometrics. Fogel’s counterfactuals and North’s institutions represent distinct economic programmes; Gutman’s criticism shows that evidence and interpretation remain contested within quantitative debate.
